Foundational Concepts & Version Control Architecture

M1_01_WHAT-IS-GIT.TXT

1. What is Git?

Git is a save button for your whole project.

Think of a video game. You save at a good moment, and if you mess up later, you load that save and carry on. Git does exactly this, but for your files.

CommitOne save point. It carries a short note like "add results".
RepositoryYour project folder, being watched by Git. People say "repo".
HistoryThe list of every save point, newest first.
TRY IT: travel through time

Click a save point, or drag the slider, to see what the folder looked like.

Tip: click the broken one and a warning pops up.

What does Git look like? Just a black window where you type short commands:

Git is a program on YOUR computer. It works even without internet.
M1_02_WHY-NEED-GIT.GIF

2. Why do we need Git?

Because report_FINAL_really_v3.docx is not a system.

Without GitCopies everywhere. Which one is the real one?
With GitOne file. Every old version is saved inside.
TRY IT: make a mess

Save a new file with a name that is already taken:

The second problem: two people, one file.

Go back in timeBroke something? Return to any earlier save.
Work togetherMany people, one project, no overwriting.
See who did whatEvery change shows who, when and why.
Git gives you undo, teamwork and a diary of changes.
M1_03_THE-CORE-PROBLEM-AND-HISTORY.TXT

3. The core problem & history

Before Git, teams kept their work safe in very messy ways.

This is called the legacy paradigm (the old way of doing things). See if any of these sound familiar:

Local backupsZip files with names like project_v1.zip and project_final_v2.zip.
Shared network drivesOne folder on the office server. Everybody edits the same files.
Email stitchingPeople email files around and someone copies the changes together by hand.
Silent overwritesYou save your version over a teammate's. Their work is gone, and nobody notices.
1990sZip backups, shared drives and emailed files.
2000SVN and other centralized tools. One server holds the history.
2005Linus Torvalds creates Git to manage the Linux kernel code.
2008GitHub launches: a website to host Git projects.
TodayGit is the standard tool for almost every software team.

Linus needed something fast that thousands of people could use at the same time. So Git was built as a distributed system:

Centralized (CVCS), like SVN

One central server holds the history. If that server goes down, nobody can commit. Everyone waits.

vs
Distributed (DVCS), like Git

Every contributor holds a full, self-contained local copy of the repository and its complete history. The server can break and work carries on.

New words
CVCS = one server has the history.
DVCS = everyone has the history.
Git was made in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, and it is distributed: everyone has the full history.
M1_04_CENTRALIZED-VS-DISTRIBUTED.EXE

4. Centralized vs Distributed Version Control Systems

Where does the history live? In one place, or everywhere?

Imagine a library book. In a centralized system there is one copy and everyone must queue for it. In a distributed system everyone owns a full photocopy of the whole book.

Centralized
One server holds the history. Everyone else has only the latest files.
Distributed (Git)
Everyone has the full history on their own laptop.

CentralizedDistributed (Git)
Server breaksNobody can save historyEveryone still has everything
No internetVery limitedKeep saving, upload later
BackupsOne copy to protectEvery copy is a backup
Git is distributed, so it is safer and works offline.
M1_05_WHAT-IS-GITHUB.DOC

5. What is GitHub?

Git is the app on your laptop. GitHub is the website where you share your project.

GitLike the notebook where you write and save your work. It stays on your computer.
GitHubLike a shelf in a public library. You put a copy there so friends can read and add to it.

This is what a project looks like on GitHub. Look at the numbers:

Git works fine without GitHub. GitLab and Bitbucket are other websites that do the same job.
Git = the tool. GitHub = the website. You use both together.
M1_06_GIT-VS-GITHUB-ECOSYSTEM.DOC

6. Ecosystem distinction: Git vs GitHub

Git and GitHub are two different things that work together.

Tool / PlatformPrimary roleExecution environmentCore capabilities
GitCLI engine & version controlYour local machineTracks file changes, manages history, branch/merge engine
GitHubCloud platform & hostingRemote servers / webRepo hosting, Pull Requests, Code Reviews, Access Control, CI/CD

Hover or tap the words in the table you are not sure about:

CLIHostingPull RequestCode ReviewAccess ControlCI/CD
Git works with no internet and no GitHub account. GitHub needs Git to send it anything.
Git = the engine on your laptop. GitHub = the website that hosts it.

M2_01_SETUP-AND-INSTALLATION.EXE

1. Git and GitHub setup and installation

Six small steps. No experience needed.

Press Next on each screen, like an installer. Try it before the session. We will also do it together.

Step 1: Meet the terminal

A terminal is a window where you type instructions (called commands) instead of clicking.

Click the Start button, type Git Bash and press Enter. (You will install it in the next step. Until then you can use Command Prompt.)

Press Cmd + Space, type Terminal, press Enter.

Press Ctrl + Alt + T, or search your apps for Terminal.

pwdWhich folder am I in?
lsList the files here
cd nameGo into a folder
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# lines starting with # are notes, do not type them
$ git --version
git version 2.xx.x

The $ is just the terminal waiting for you. Do not type it. Type the rest and press Enter.

Step 2: Install Git

Pick your computer type and follow the numbers.

1

Go to git-scm.com/download/win. The download starts by itself. If not, click "Click here to download".

2

Open the downloaded file (Git-2.xx.x-64-bit.exe). If Windows asks "Do you want to allow this app to make changes?" click Yes.

3

You will see many screens. On almost all of them, just click Next. The default choices are fine.

4

One screen is worth reading: "Adjusting the name of the initial branch". Pick "Override..." and keep the name main.

5

Click Install, wait for the green bar, then Finish.

6

Click Start, type Git Bash, press Enter. That black window is your terminal for the whole workshop.

1

Open Terminal: Cmd + Space, type Terminal, Enter.

2

Type git --version and press Enter.

3

If a box asks about the command line developer tools, click Install and wait a few minutes.

4

Type git --version again. A version number means you are done.

5

Optional: if you use Homebrew, brew install git also works.

1

Open the terminal: Ctrl + Alt + T.

2

Type sudo apt update and press Enter. Type your password when asked. Nothing shows while you type it, and that is normal.

3

Type sudo apt install git, press Enter, and type y when it asks. (Fedora: sudo dnf install git.)

4

Check with git --version.

Step 3: Check that it works

Open your terminal and type the command, then press Enter.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git --version
git version 2.43.0
You see "git version ..."Perfect! Go to the next step. Your numbers may differ, that is fine.
You see an errorClose the terminal and open a new one. Still stuck? See the last step.

Step 4: Make a GitHub account

This happens in your web browser. It is free.

1

Go to github.com and click Sign up.

2

Type your email, make a password, pick a username.

3

Solve the small puzzle, then type the code GitHub emails you.

4

Choose the Free plan. Skip any extra questions.

Your username is public and appears in your project links, so pick something you are happy to show.

Step 5: Tell Git who you are

Every save point is signed with a name and email. You do this once per computer. Change the name and email to yours.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git config --global user.name "Nishita Kumari"
$ git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main

Nothing is printed when it works. No news is good news. To double check:

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git config --list
user.name=Nishita Kumari
user.email=you@example.com
init.defaultbranch=main
Use the same email as your GitHub account. The first time you upload, a browser window opens to sign in. Click Authorize. Your account password will not work in the terminal.

Step 6: Checklist and fixes

Tick everything off. If something went wrong, open a problem box.

Tick what you have done

Common problems. Click one.

"git is not recognized" / "command not found"
Close every terminal and open a new one. On Windows use Git Bash. Still failing? Run the installer again with the recommended choices.
"Please tell me who you are"
You skipped the name and email step. Run the two git config --global commands.
A box asks for developer tools (Mac)
Normal. Click Install and wait, then run git --version.
The GitHub email never arrived
Check spam, wait a minute, click Resend, and check the email you typed.
Password rejected when pushing
Use the browser sign-in window that opens. If there is none, create a personal access token in GitHub Settings, Developer settings.
M2_02_ENVIRONMENT-CONFIGURATION.EXE

2. Installation & environment configuration

Check Git is installed, then tell it who you are before your first snapshot.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Verify installation
git --version

# Set global identity (stored in ~/.gitconfig)
git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"

# Set main as default branch name across all new repos
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Inspect configuration parameters
git config --list --show-origin

What each part means:

--globalApplies to every project on this computer, not just one.
~/.gitconfigThe settings file in your home folder (~) where --global settings are saved.
init.defaultBranch mainNew repos start on a branch called main.
--show-originShows which settings file each setting comes from.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git config --list --show-origin
file:/home/you/.gitconfig    user.name=Your Full Name
file:/home/you/.gitconfig    user.email=your.email@example.com
file:/home/you/.gitconfig    init.defaultbranch=main
file:.git/config             core.bare=false
Forgot this step? Git refuses to commit and says Author identity unknown. Try it in the Practice Lab!
Set your name and email once per computer, before your first commit.
M2_03_THE-4-GIT-STATES.GIF

3. The 4 Git internal states & data lifecycle

To master Git, learn the four places a change can live.

Your files move from the folder you edit, into a waiting area, into saved history, and finally up to GitHub. Try it: press the buttons in order and watch index.html travel.

TRY IT: MOVE A CHANGE THROUGH THE 4 STATES

Press Edit a file to begin, or click a box to read what it is.

StateWhat it is
Working DirectoryFiles currently being added, deleted, or edited on disk.
Staging Area (Index)A draft file inside .git/ that collects selected modifications scheduled for the next snapshot.
Local RepositoryThe local .git directory containing all blob objects, commit trees, and reference pointers.
Remote RepositoryThe centralized server hosting shared repository objects for team sync (for example GitHub).
Go deeper: two kinds of git restore

git restore --staged file takes a file out of the staging area but keeps your edits.

git restore file throws away your unsaved edits in the working directory and puts back the last saved version. Careful: those edits are gone for good.

Edit → git add → git commit → git push.

M3_03_BASIC-GIT-COMMANDS.GIF

3. Basic Git commands: git init, add, commit, status, log

Think of packing a parcel.

git addPut things in the box.
git commitSeal the box and write a label on it.
git logLook at all the boxes you sealed.
TRY IT: follow a file

Press Next step and watch a file travel.

Working folderwhere you edit files
Staging areathe box, ready to seal
Local repoyour saved history
GitHubthe online copy
$ mkdir recipes

The five commands. Click a card to flip it.

git initclick to flip
Start watching this folder. Once per project.
git statusclick to flip
What changed? What is ready to save?
git addclick to flip
Pick changes for the next save point.
git commit -m "note"click to flip
Save the picked changes with a note.
git logclick to flip
List all past saves, newest first.

All together, line by line:

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ mkdir recipes
$ cd recipes
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in recipes/.git/
$ echo "Pasta" > pasta.txt
$ git status
Untracked files:
    pasta.txt
$ git add pasta.txt
$ git commit -m "Add pasta recipe"
[main a3f9c21] Add pasta recipe
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git log --oneline
a3f9c21 Add pasta recipe
Why a staging box? You changed five files but only two belong together. Add those two, save them, and the other three wait for their own save.
M3_04_INIT-STATUS-STAGE-COMMIT.EXE

4. Initializing, status, staging & committing

Six commands do most of your daily work.

1. Initializing & checking status

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Initialize tracking inside a directory
git init

# View status of tracked/untracked files
git status

# View status in compact/short format
git status -s

git status -s prints two letters per file. Hover or tap each code:

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git status -s
?? notes.txt
 M index.html
M  styles.css
A  app.js
 D old.txt
Left letter = staging area.
Right letter = working folder.

2. Staging & committing

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Stage specific files
git add index.html styles.css

# Stage all modified and new untracked files
git add .

# Commit staged snapshot with an imperative-mood message
git commit -m "add user authentication middleware"

# Combine staging tracked files and committing into one step
git commit -am "fix layout alignment in navbar"
git add . then git commit -m

Stages everything, including brand-new untracked files, then commits.

vs
git commit -am

Stages and commits in one go, but only files Git already tracks. New files are left out!

Imperative mood means writing the message like an order: "add login", not "added login". Read it as "If applied, this commit will add login".

git init once, then: git status, git add, git commit, again and again.
M3_05_LOG-HISTORY-AND-INSPECTION.TXT

5. Log history & inspection

git log is your project's diary. Four ways to read it:

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Inspect chronological log
git log

# View compact single-line history
git log --oneline

# View single-line log with graph representation of branches
git log --oneline --graph --all

# View changes made in the last 3 commits
git log -p -3
TRY IT: CLICK A TAB TO SEE WHAT EACH ONE PRINTS
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git log
commit 9f2c1ab7e4d0c3b2a1f9e8d7c6b5a4f3e2d1c0b9 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Nishita <you@example.com>
Date:   Mon Nov 2 10:15:00 2026 +0530

    add navbar styles

commit 4d8e2f1c0b9a8f7e6d5c4b3a2f1e0d9c8b7a6f5e
Author: Nishita <you@example.com>
Date:   Mon Nov 2 09:40:00 2026 +0530

    add home page

Full details of every commit: id, author, date and message. Press q to quit the list.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git log --oneline
9f2c1ab (HEAD -> main) add navbar styles
4d8e2f1 add home page
1a2b3c4 initial commit

One line per commit: a short id and the message. The easiest to read.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
*   c7d8e9f (HEAD -> main) merge feature/dashboard
|\
| * 5e6f7a8 (feature/dashboard) add dashboard chart
* | 9f2c1ab add navbar styles
|/
* 4d8e2f1 add home page

Draws the branches as lines. --all shows every branch, not just the one you are on.

GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git log -p -3
commit 9f2c1ab (HEAD -> main)
    add navbar styles

diff --git a/styles.css b/styles.css
--- a/styles.css
+++ b/styles.css
@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@
 nav {
-  color: black;
+  color: navy;
+  padding: 8px;
 }
... (2 more commits)

-p shows the patch (the exact lines changed). -3 limits it to the last 3 commits.

Stuck inside a long log? Press q to get your prompt back.
git log --oneline is the one you will use most.

File Exclusions & Directory Handling

1. .gitignore2. Writing .gitignore rules3. Tracking empty directoriesKnowledge check
M4_01_GITIGNORE.TXT

1. Understanding .gitignore

.gitignore is the list of things you do not pack in the suitcase.

Secret passwords, huge files, junk your tools create. List them in a plain text file named .gitignore and Git pretends they do not exist.

TRY IT: ignore some files

Click a file to ignore or un-ignore it.

LineMeaning
.envIgnore this exact file
*.logIgnore every file ending in .log
node_modules/Ignore this whole folder
Create it before your first commit. A secret that was already committed stays in the history, even if you delete the file later.




M4_02_WRITING-GITIGNORE-RULES.TXT


2. Writing .gitignore rules


Prevent temporary files, build artifacts and secrets from ever being tracked.
.GITIGNORE
# Ignore build outputs
/dist/
/build/
*.exe

# Ignore dependencies
node_modules/
/vendor/

# Ignore environment variables & secrets (CRITICAL)
.env
.env.local
*.pem

# Ignore OS system files
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
PatternMeaning
/dist/The dist folder at the top of the project only (the leading / means "from the project root").
*.exeAny file ending in .exe, in any folder.
node_modules/Any folder called node_modules, wherever it is.
.envFiles holding passwords and API keys. Critical.
*.pemCertificate and private key files.
.DS_Store / Thumbs.dbJunk files that macOS and Windows create on their own.
Oops: I already committed .env
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Remove a file from tracking that was accidentally committed, without deleting it locally
git rm --cached .env
.env is tracked
  • 📄 .env tracked: the secret goes to GitHub
  • 📄 app.py tracked
Every push uploads your secret key.
➜
git rm --cached .env + .gitignore
  • 📄 .env ignored, still on your laptop
  • 📄 app.py tracked
Commit this change, then push.
Warning: the old commits still contain the key. If a real secret was ever pushed, change the password or key straight away.
Write .gitignore before your first commit. Secrets never go in Git.




M4_03_TRACKING-EMPTY-DIRECTORIES.EXE


3. Tracking empty directories


Git tracks file contents, not empty folders.
An empty uploads/ or logs/ folder simply disappears when someone clones your project. The fix: put a tiny placeholder file called .gitkeep inside it.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
mkdir -p logs
touch logs/.gitkeep
git add logs/.gitkeep
git commit -m "add logs directory structure"
mkdir -p logsMake the folder (-p: no error if it already exists).
touch logs/.gitkeepCreate an empty placeholder file inside it.
git add + commitNow Git has a file to track, so the folder is kept.
No .gitkeep
my-app/
├ app.py
└ (logs/ missing after clone)
➜
With .gitkeep
my-app/
├ app.py
└ logs/
  └ .gitkeep
.gitkeep is just a habit people agreed on. Git does not treat the name specially: any file would work.
Empty folder? Add a .gitkeep file inside it.

M5_01_INTRODUCTION-TO-BRANCHES.TXT


1. Introduction to branches


A branch is a draft copy where you can experiment safely.
You wrote a perfect essay and want to try a risky new ending. You would not edit the only copy. You would make a draft. If the ending is great, you keep it. If not, you throw the draft away.
SafeWhatever you break on a branch never touches main.
ParallelEach teammate works on their own branch at the same time.
main is the official version. Branches are side roads.




M5_02_CREATING-AND-SWITCHING-BRANCHES.GIF


2. Creating and switching branches


Three commands. That is all.
git branchList my branches. The * marks where I am.
git switch -c nameMake a new branch and move onto it.
git switch nameMove to a branch that already exists.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git branch
* main
$ git switch -c feature/login
Switched to a new branch 'feature/login'
$ git branch
* feature/login
  main
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
No spaces in branch names. Use dashes: add-login-page. Older guides use git checkout -b, which does the same job.




M5_03_ISOLATED-BRANCH-WORKFLOWS.EXE


3. Isolated branch workflows


Branches are cheap, lightweight, moveable pointers to specific commits.
A branch is not a copy of your files. It is a small sticky label that points at one commit, and it moves forward each time you commit.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# List all local branches
git branch

# Create a new feature branch
git branch feature/user-profile

# Switch to target branch
git switch feature/user-profile

# Shortcut: Create and switch to a new branch in one command
git switch -c feature/dashboard
git branch name only creates the branch. You are still on the old one until you git switch.
Merging strategies
Integrate completed feature branches into the principal code path (usually main):
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Switch to target base branch
git switch main

# Execute merge operation
git merge feature/dashboard
Create, switch, work, switch back to main, merge.




M5_04_BRANCHING-AND-MERGING.EXE


4. Branching and merging


When your branch is ready, you merge it back into main.
TRY IT: build a branch tree
Press the buttons in order: 1, 2, then 3.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
$ git switch main
$ git merge feature/login
Merge made. 2 files changed.
$ git branch -d feature/login   # tidy up
Go to main first, then merge the branch into it.




M5_05_MERGE-CONFLICTS-AND-RESOLUTION.TXT


5. Merge Conflicts and their resolution


Two people edit the same line. Git asks you to choose.
This is normal, not a disaster. Git simply cannot guess whose line is better.
The file Git shows you
<<<<<<< HEAD
title = "Home"
=======
title = "Welcome"
>>>>>>> feature/login
Top part = yours. Bottom part = theirs.
You are the referee
title = ???
Press the button. A warning pops up and you decide.
How to fix one in real life
1
Spot itgit status lists files that are "both modified".
›
2
EditKeep what you want. Delete the three marker lines.
›
3
Stagegit add file
›
4
Finishgit commit




M5_06_RESOLVING-MERGE-CONFLICTS.TXT


6. Resolving merge conflicts: the full sequence


When parallel commits edit the exact same lines, Git stops and adds conflict markers.
INDEX.HTML (HTML)
<<<<<<< HEAD
<h1>Dashboard - Main Branch Version</h1>
=======
<h1>Dashboard - Feature Branch Version</h1>
>>>>>>> feature/dashboard
MarkerMeans
<<<<<<< HEADStart of your version (the branch you are on).
=======The dividing line.
>>>>>>> feature/dashboardEnd of their version (the branch you are merging in).
Resolution sequence:
1
OpenOpen the conflicted files in VS Code or a text editor.
›
2
EditKeep the output you want. Remove the marker lines <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>.
›
3
Stagegit add <file>
›

=======

Changed your mind halfway? git merge --abort puts everything back as it was before the merge.
Edit, remove the markers, git add, git commit.




M5_07_STASHING-TEMPORARY-WORK.GIF


7. Stashing temporary work


Shelve unfinished work without making a half-baked commit.
You are halfway through something and need to switch branches to fix a bug. git stash puts your unsaved changes on a shelf (a stack) and gives you a clean folder.
GIT BASH / TERMINAL
# Save uncommitted changes to stash stack
git stash

# Save stash with descriptive label
git stash save "wip: shopping cart checkout logic"

# List all stored stashes
git stash list

# Apply most recent stash and remove it from stash stack
git stash pop

# Apply a specific stash without dropping it
git stash apply stash@{1}
Correction: git stash save is the older form. It still works, but newer Git prefers git stash push -m "wip: shopping cart checkout logic", which does the same thing.
TRY IT: THE STASH SHELF
Working directory
Stash stack
    

    

    git stash pop
    Brings the newest stash back and removes it from the stack.
    vs
    git stash apply stash@{1}
    Brings back stash number 1 and keeps it on the stack too.
    stash = shelf it. pop = take it back.
    

    

    M5_08_REBASING-VS-MERGING.EXE
    

    8. Rebasing vs. merging
    

    Two ways to bring main's new work into your branch: merge or rebase.
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    # Rebase feature branch onto updated main branch to achieve a linear commit line
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
    TRY IT: SEE THE DIFFERENCE
    Merge
    Preserves full historical context and non-linear branch history via explicit merge commits. Nothing is rewritten.
    vs
    Rebase
    Re-applies your local commits on top of the target base branch, yielding a clean, linear commit timeline. Your commits get new ids.
    Golden rule: never rebase public/shared branches. Rebase rewrites commits, so teammates who already have the old ones get into a mess.
    Go deeper: if a rebase hits a conflict
    Git pauses on the commit that clashes. Fix the file, then git add file and git rebase --continue. To skip that commit use git rebase --skip; to give up and go back to how things were, git rebase --abort. All of these work in the Practice Lab.
    Merge keeps the story as it happened. Rebase tidies it into a straight line.
    

    

    M5_09_VERSION-RELEASE-TAGGING.TXT
    

    9. Version release tagging
    

    A tag is a permanent name for one important commit, like a release.
    a1b2c3🏷 v1.0.0d4main
    Branches move forward with every commit. A tag stays stuck to its commit forever, so v1.0.0 always means exactly that release.
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    # Create an annotated release tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "production release version 1.0.0"

# List all tags
git tag

# Push tags to remote server
git push origin --tags
    -aAnnotated tag: stores who made it, when, and a message. Best for releases.
    -m "..."The tag's message.
    v1.0.0A version number: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
    git push on its own does not upload tags. You need git push origin --tags.
    Tag your releases: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "...", then push the tags.

    Remote Infrastructure & GitHub Integration
    Connecting your laptop to GitHub
    

    1. Push, Pull and Clone2. Remote repositories3. Linking local repositories to remote hosts4. Fetching vs. pullingKnowledge check
    

    

    M6_01_PUSH-PULL-AND-CLONE.DOC
    

    1. Push, Pull and Clone
    

    Your laptop and GitHub are two copies. These commands post work between them.
    git pushPost your new commits UP to GitHub.
    git pullBring new commits DOWN from GitHub.
    git cloneDownload a whole project for the first time.
    Your first push, step by step
    1
    On GitHub, create a new repo. If your project already has commits, leave "Add a README" unticked.
    2
    Click the green Code button and copy the web address.
    3
    In your terminal, inside your project folder: git remote add origin PASTE-THE-ADDRESS
    4
    Name your branch main: git branch -M main
    5
    Upload: git push -u origin main. A browser window may open. Click Authorize.
    6
    Refresh the GitHub page. Your files are there!
    Cloning is easier. The link comes from the green Code button:
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    $ git clone https://github.com/user/recipes.git
Cloning into 'recipes'... done.
$ cd recipes
$ git pull
Already up to date.
    Push = upload. Pull = download the latest. Clone = download everything once.
    

    

    M6_02_UNDERSTANDING-REMOTE-REPOSITORIES.EXE
    

    2. Understanding remote repositories
    

    A remote is the online copy, saved in your contacts under a nickname.
    The usual nickname is origin. Your laptop even remembers where GitHub was the last time you checked, as origin/main.
    git remote -vShow my remotes and their addresses.
    git fetchCheck what is new online, but do not touch my files.
    git pullFetch, and also bring the new work into my files.
    git push -u origin main uploads and remembers the link. After that, plain git push and git pull know where to go.
    Remote = the online copy. origin = its nickname.
    

    

    M6_03_LINKING-LOCAL-TO-REMOTE.EXE
    

    3. Linking local repositories to remote hosts
    

    Connect the repo on your laptop to an empty repo on GitHub.
    No repo on GitHub yet? Make one first: in the Browser press + New repository (just like github.com/new), or type gh repo create my-project --public. GitHub then shows you the link to use below. Typed the wrong link? Fix it with git remote set-url origin <link>.
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    # Link local repository to remote host
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repository-name.git

# Verify configured remote endpoints
git remote -v

# Push main branch to remote and set tracking upstream (-u)
git push -u origin main
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    $ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/username/repository-name.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/username/repository-name.git (push)
    originThe nickname for the GitHub address. You could pick another name, but everyone uses origin.
    -uShort for --set-upstream: remembers that local main goes with origin/main. Afterwards, plain git push is enough.
    https://...Copy it from the green Code button on GitHub. The first push opens a browser window to sign in.
    remote add once, push -u once, then just git push.
    

    

    M6_04_FETCHING-VS-PULLING.GIF
    

    4. Fetching vs. pulling
    

    fetch looks. pull looks and brings it in.
    GIT BASH / TERMINAL
    # Fetch: Downloads new remote commits and references without modifying working directory
git fetch origin

# Pull: Executes 'git fetch' followed immediately by 'git merge' into local branch
git pull origin main
    TRY IT: WATCH WHAT EACH ONE CHANGES
    GitHuborigin
    origin/mainyour laptop's memory of GitHub
    mainyour branch & files
    

    git fetch
    Downloads new commits into origin/main. Your files do not change. Safe any time.
    vs
    git pull
    git fetch + git merge. Your main and your files are updated.
    Go deeper: pull with rebase
    git pull --rebase fetches, then rebases your new commits on top instead of making a merge commit. The result is a straight history. You can try it in the Practice Lab.
    Not sure? git fetch first, look, then git pull.

        1. Forking repositories
        

        A fork is your own copy of someone else's project, on GitHub.
        Like photocopying a recipe book to your own shelf. You can improve your copy freely, then suggest your best changes back to the owner with a pull request.
        Where is the Fork button? Top right of any project page:
        Fork = copy on GitHub. Clone = copy on your laptop. Do both, then open a pull request.
        

        

        M8_02_FORK-AND-PR-MODEL.GIF
        

        2. Open source contribution model (Fork & PR)
        

        How you help with someone else's project, even without permission to push to it.
        TRY IT: FOLLOW A CONTRIBUTION
        

        Press the steps in order.
        1
        ForkCreate a personal server-side copy of an upstream repository on GitHub.
        ›
        2
        Clone & BranchClone your fork locally and create a topic branch (feature/bugfix).
        ›
        3
        Commit & PushMake small local commits and push the branch to your GitHub fork (origin).
        ›

        Pull RequestOpen a PR on GitHub comparing your fork's topic branch against the original repository's main.
        GIT BASH / TERMINAL
        git clone https://github.com/you/website.git
cd website
git switch -c fix/typo-in-footer
git commit -am "fix typo in footer"
git push -u origin fix/typo-in-footer
        UpstreamThe original project.
        OriginYour fork on GitHub.
        Topic branchOne branch per fix.

        ForkAnyone can copy it and send a pull request. Good for open source.

        9
        Production Best Practices & AI-Enhanced Tooling

        M9_01_BEST-PRACTICES.DOC
        

        1. Repository management best practices
        

        Good habits make a project easy for everyone, including you in six months.
        Save small and oftenOne idea per commit, not fifty files at once.
        Write clear messagesSay what changed and why.
        Pull before you startAlways get the latest work first.
        Use branchesNever work straight on main in a team.
        Never commit secretsPasswords and keys go in .gitignore.
        Review each otherUse pull requests so someone checks your work.
        AvoidPrefer
        "fix""Fix login button on mobile"
        "changes""Add search to recipe page"
        50 files in one commitOne idea per commit
        Committing straight to mainBranch, then pull request
        

        

        M9_02_PROFESSIONAL-GIT-BEST-PRACTICES.DOC
        

        2. Professional Git best practices
        

        Four habits that make you look like a professional.
        Imperative mood commitsWrite subject lines like an order: add rate limiting to login endpoint, not added rate limiting.
        Micro-commitsKeep commits atomic: each one is one logically complete unit of work.
        Short-lived branchesMerge feature branches back quickly, so they do not drift far from main (big divergence = big conflicts).
        Keep secrets outNever commit passwords, API keys or certificates (people call this secret hygiene). Use pre-commit hooks (git-secrets, trufflehog) to scan the staged changes automatically.
        KNOWLEDGE CHECK
        1. Which commit subject line is in the imperative mood?
        2. You fixed a bug AND renamed 40 files. How many commits?
        One giant commit
        * 3f9a1c2 changes
  52 files changed
        ➜
        Micro-commits
        * 8c1d2e3 fix crash on empty cart
* 7b0c1d2 rename css classes to kebab-case
* 6a9b0c1 add search box to recipe page
        GIT BASH / TERMINAL (WITH A SECRET-SCANNING HOOK)
        # a pre-commit hook scans what you staged, before the commit happens
$ git commit -m "add payment api"
[ERROR] Matched one or more prohibited patterns
.env:2: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=AKIA...
Possible mitigations:
- Mark false positives as allowed
- Remove the secret and try again
        A leaked key must be cancelled and replaced, even if you delete it from the code later. It stays in the history.
        Small commits, clear orders, short branches, no secrets.

        4. Creating and maintaining a README file
        

        The README is the front cover of your project.
        GitHub shows it on your repo page. It is a file called README.md. The .md means Markdown: headings and lists written with simple symbols.
        What you type

2. Open index.html

        M9_05_AI-ASSISTED-GIT-WORKFLOWS.EXE
        

        5. AI-assisted Git workflows
        

        AI can help with Git, as long as you stay in charge.
        1. Automated commit messages
        AI extensions in VS Code (the ✨ button in the commit box) or CLI wrappers read your staged diff and suggest a summary:
        1
        Stagegit add your change.
        ›
        2
        DiffThe tool reads git diff --staged.
        ›
        3
        SuggestAI writes a commit message.
        ›
        4
        You checkEdit it if it is wrong, then commit.
        GIT BASH / TERMINAL
        $ git diff --staged
-  if (cart.length > 0) checkout()
+  if (cart.length > 0 && user) checkout()

# suggested message:
#   fix checkout running without a signed-in user
$ git commit -m "fix checkout running without a signed-in user"
        2. AI feature branch sandboxing
        Isolate radical AI-generated experiments inside a dedicated throwaway branch, review them, and cherry-pick only the good commits into your real branch.
        GIT BASH / TERMINAL
        # 1. a throwaway branch just for the AI experiment
git switch -c feature/ai-refactor-experiment
# ...let the AI make changes, commit them, test them...
git log --oneline

# 2. back to main, and copy only the commit that works
git switch main
git cherry-pick 4f2a9c1

# 3. throw the experiment away
git branch -D feature/ai-refactor-experiment
        Never paste secrets, passwords or private code into an AI chat. And read every AI change before you commit it: you are the one signing it.
        Let AI suggest. You review, you decide, you commit.
